title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: A utility pledge on data center bills, plus moratoria spreading across Michigan

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy, the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Saturday, July 25, and we're starting with a fresh pledge from Indiana Michigan Power that aims to keep residential customers off the hook for new data center power lines.
That sounds like a big shift in how these projects get paid for. What's behind the pledge and how might it play out for folks in southwest Michigan?
Indiana Michigan Power serves parts of the southwest corner of the state and they signed on to this commitment amid rising worries that AI-driven demand could push up electric bills statewide.
Why is this pledge coming now? Have utilities been passing costs along in other places already?
Exactly. We've seen similar infrastructure needs pop up with DTE projects, and ratepayers there have already picked up some added charges tied to earlier builds.
So this is the utility trying to get ahead of the backlash before it hits their own customers?
It looks that way. Local officials and consumer groups are now watching closely to see whether the promise holds when the actual rate cases come before regulators.
What kind of money are we talking about here? Even one big data center can pull hundreds of megawatts.
Right, and those lines and substations don't come cheap. The pledge is meant to make sure those upgrades don't land on household bills the way they have elsewhere.
How does this fit into the wider pattern we've seen this week with townships hitting pause buttons?
It's part of the same tension. Places like Garfield Township froze new projects yesterday after a sloppy application, and Delta County did the same on Thursday over noise, water, and grid strain.
Those pauses give local leaders time to write actual rules. Does the I&M pledge change the math for communities still weighing projects?
It could ease some fears on the power side, but water use and noise complaints are still very much on the table in places like Dowagiac and Wixom.
Speaking of water, these facilities can draw millions of gallons. How does that square with the pledge focusing only on electric rates?
The pledge is narrow, just on power lines. Towns still have to sort out their own water and zoning concerns, which is why we're seeing so many moratoria.
What's the history here? Have we seen utilities make similar promises before?
Not exactly like this one, but the broader fight over who pays for data center infrastructure has been heating up as more hyperscale projects land in Michigan.
And the players? We have the utilities, the tech companies like Oracle, and then the townships and counties.
Yes, and residents who show up at meetings worried about their bills, their wells, and their property values.
What happens next with this pledge? Does it go into effect immediately or does it need approval?
It will get tested in upcoming rate proceedings. Consumer groups plan to hold the company to its word there.
Meanwhile other utilities like DTE are highlighting data center growth as a profit driver in their latest numbers.
That's the flip side. More demand can boost earnings, but it also means more pressure on the grid that often circles back to ratepayers.
Calhoun County is debating its own year-long halt over jobs versus power strain. How does the I&M move affect that conversation?
It gives commissioners one more data point, but the core worries about hundreds of megawatts and millions of gallons of water remain local decisions.
Augusta Township is also close to a vote on rules for a big Oracle-scale project pulling from the same DTE area as Saline.
That outcome will show how much new load hits ratepayers and whether the township gets meaningful revenue in return.
Saline Township flipped this week and restored Oracle's shot at a big tax break after earlier limits.
Yes, after company lobbying. Residents there now face the prospect of forgoing years of property tax revenue on a multibillion-dollar project.
And Wixom kept its pause in place to protect residents from power strain and noise.
City council rejected lifting the moratorium early, citing health and resource risks that could raise costs for locals.
Dowagiac residents are still dealing with humming from an operating center's cooling systems and exploring legal options.
Persistent noise complaints like that show the quality-of-life side of these projects that doesn't always show up in the rate discussion.
The MLive map that launched this week lets people track every active fight by township and county.
It surfaces megawatts demanded and potential tax deals in real time so residents can compare what's happening near them.
With all these pauses and pledges, is the overall pace of data center development slowing down?
It's fragmenting. Some places are hitting the brakes while others negotiate terms, and the I&M pledge is one more variable in that mix.
What should listeners watch for in the coming weeks?
Rate case filings, any new moratorium votes, and whether the pledge actually shows up in the numbers utilities file with regulators.
And on the ground, more public comments at township meetings where these projects get decided one by one.
Exactly. The big picture is that communities are trying to get ahead of costs before projects lock in.
Do we have any sense yet how many townships have already paused or passed rules?
At least a handful this week alone, from Garfield and Delta to Wixom and Calhoun, with more likely to follow as applications keep coming in.
And the stakes for farmland and small towns keep coming up. Converting fields or straining rural grids changes the character of those places.
That's the tension: promised jobs and tax revenue versus real impacts on daily life and long-term costs.
The pledge tries to address one piece, the electric side, but leaves water and zoning to locals.
And that's why we're seeing so much local action even as utilities make statewide commitments.
What happens if the pledge doesn't hold in a rate case?
Consumer groups would likely push back hard, and it could become a political issue for the utility going forward.
Meanwhile the MLive tracker gives everyone a way to follow the map of these fights in real time.
It's a useful tool for anyone wondering how projects near them stack up against battles elsewhere.
So the I&M move is a signal, but the real test will be in the details of those rate filings.
And in whether other utilities follow suit or stick with the current cost-recovery model.
Either way, residents in the I&M territory get at least a temporary assurance on the power side.
For now. The proof will come when the first big projects hit their service area.
Shifting to quick hits, Garfield Township supervisors voted yesterday to block new data centers for at least a year after an incomplete application.
Residents near that site now have breathing room to sort out concerns over power lines, water, and property values.
DTE's latest numbers show data center growth driving earnings, which often means more infrastructure costs that can hit households.
Michigan ratepayers have already seen some of those charges from earlier projects in the territory.
Calhoun County commissioners are weighing their own year-long moratorium after hearing worries about electricity and whether jobs will benefit local taxpayers.
A pause there would delay projects drawing hundreds of megawatts and millions of gallons of water.
Augusta Township is nearing a vote on zoning and tax terms for a large proposal pulling power from the same DTE area as Saline.
The outcome will shape how much new load hits ratepayers and how much revenue the township keeps.
In Cass County, Dowagiac residents are reporting ongoing noise from an operating data center's cooling systems and looking at legal steps.
Those complaints highlight the day-to-day quality-of-life issues that go beyond just rates.
Saline Township reversed an earlier limit and restored Oracle's path to a big tax break after lobbying.
That leaves residents facing the loss of years of property tax revenue on a multibillion-dollar project.
Delta County voted Thursday to ban new data centers for a year after residents raised noise, water, and rural grid concerns.
The moratorium gives officials time to write permanent zoning rules before any hyperscale project moves forward.
The new MLive map tracks every active data center fight across the state by township and county.
It shows megawatts and tax deals in real time so people can see the stakes near them.
And in Oakland County, Wixom city council kept its moratorium in place to shield residents from power strain and noise risks.
They rejected an early end, citing potential health and resource costs that could raise resident bills.
On deck this weekend, with it being Saturday, no major public hearings are scheduled that we're tracking.
The MLive map is the best place to check for any last-minute additions or next week's agendas.
Listeners can keep an eye on the tracker for updates as more townships weigh their own rules.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Indiana Michigan Power Pledges to Shield Ratepayers from Data Center Costs
